title: Tokenization-bound quant latency coupling probe
content:
Summary:
This note captures an exploratory investigation into how tokenization characteristics interact with low-precision quantized kernels to produce surprisingly non-linear latency effects. The goal: surface actionable profiling signals that explain tail latency spikes observed on INT8/AWQ kernels for short versus medium prompt shapes.

Motivation / context:
- Several SRE alerts in late March reported 99th percentile latency regressions when we rolled an AWQ kernel variant for a small-hosted model (S-3).
- Initial throughput benches looked fine, but real traffic showed a spike correlated with short user prompts (~3–15 tokens) and high variety in token-length distributions (mixed token-width due to emoji / CJK / subword tokens).
- Hypothesis: tokenization produces variable internal sequence lengths and byte-alignment that interacts with kernel packing/widening heuristics in low-precision paths (INT8/AWQ/FP8), causing more kernel launches or worse vector lane utilization.

High-level questions:
1) For a fixed logical prompt length (in tokens), how much does the underlying token byte-length / subword distribution affect per-token latency on different quant kernels?
2) Are there identifiable micro-patterns (e.g., high prevalence of long subwords, surrogate pairs) that cause kernel selection or codepath divergence leading to tail latency?
3) Can we cheaply detect offending tokenization patterns at the request edge and apply local mitigation (prefix caching, forced batching, lightweight prefix pad) without full model fallback?

Experiment matrix:
- Models: S-3-small (decoder-only 6B), M-7 (7B ref), baseline L-13-lite for control.
- Quant variants: FP16 baseline, INT8-GPTQ, AWQ-3b, FP8-alpha (internal tuning 0.7).
- Kernels: vector-tiling-v1, lane-pack-v2, strided-simd-v1 (used by AWQ), fallback-emu (slow but correctness reference).
- Token mixes (synthetic corpuses):
  A) short-english: avg 4 tokens, mostly ascii, small subword sizes
  B) emoji-heavy: avg 4 tokens, includes multi-byte emoji sequences, surrogate pairs
  C) cjk: avg 4 tokens, wide codepoints, fewer subwords but longer bytes/token
  D) mixed-medium: 12 tokens, mixture of long english words and code snippets (backticks)
  E) long-subword: artificially concatenated long tokens (tests kernel packing edge)
- Workload modes: single-request latency (P95/P99), small-batch (batch size 4), concurrency sweep (1–32).

Instrumentation additions for this probe:
- Tokenizer trace: record (tokens_count, avg_bytes_per_token, max_bytes_token, unicode_category_histogram) per request in local trace headers.
- Kernel entry log: micro-timestamped events for kernel selection, launch_count, tiling_dimensions, vector_utilization_estimate (sampled every 128 tokens).
- Lightweight fingerprint: 1-bit per request flag if tokenization contains surrogate pairs or non-latin scripts.

Key findings (short):
1) For INT8-GPTQ and AWQ-3b kernels, average per-token latency increased 10–25% for corpuses B and C (emoji and CJK) compared to short-english, even when token count was identical.
2) The latency delta tracked strongly with max_bytes_token and with presence of surrogate pairs. When max_bytes_token > 10 bytes we saw an increased kernel launch_count (extra tiling pass).
3) vector-tiling-v1 shows a worst-case penalty on lanes utilization when token byte-length distribution is skewed; lane-pack-v2 is more robust but has slightly higher steady-state overhead.
4) FP8-alpha did not show the same launch_count behavior, but had higher average latency than FP16 baseline for mixed-medium prompts due to additional bookkeeping for stochastic rounding path.
5) Small-batch (bs=4) amortization reduces delta but does not remove the 99th percentile jitter for emoji-heavy inputs.

Representative microbench snapshot (S-3, avg logical tokens=4, concurrency=8):
- short-english: FP16 baseline p99=68ms, INT8-GPTQ p99=75ms, AWQ-3b p99=82ms
- emoji-heavy: FP16 baseline p99=72ms, INT8-GPTQ p99=95ms, AWQ-3b p99=110ms
- cjk: FP16 baseline p99=74ms, INT8-GPTQ p99=92ms, AWQ-3b p99=108ms
(These are field-like microbench numbers — see linked artifacts for raw traces.)

Observed kernel behavior (from kernel entry logs):
- When max_bytes_token <= 6 the kernel chooses pack-fast path: single launch, good vector occupancy (~85%).
- When max_bytes_token > 6 the scheduler sometimes falls back to multi-pass tiling that splits the sequence into micro-tiles; this doubles launch_count in many cases and occupancy drops to ~40–55% for vector-tiling-v1.
- lane-pack-v2 mitigates the falloff by packing smaller lanes more tightly but adds a 6–8us per-launch overhead, so it wins for heavy-skew workloads but loses slightly on pure ascii.

Hypotheses validated / invalidated:
- Validated: Token byte-length (and unicode structure) is a principal factor driving a kernel-switching behavior that affects latency tails on low-precision kernels.
- Invalidated: We initially thought AWQ internal quant state (per-head scale quirks) was the main cause — traces show launch_count and tiling as the primary mechanism, not quant math divergence.

Quick mitigations tried (and results):
1) Edge-level detection + prefix-pad to 8 bytes-per-token estimate: reduced kernel switches by ~60% for emoji-heavy inputs, p99 improved by ~25% for AWQ paths. Cost: additional tokens sent (controlled pad of minimal size) — small effect on quality but OK for system prompts.
2) Opportunistic small-batching (hold 5–10ms): reduces P99 but increases median by a few ms — tradeoff acceptable for non-interactive use-cases only.
3) Kernel config flag: force lane-pack-v2 for models with high emoji/CJK traffic — worked well in controlled experiments; server-side policy required to be robust to load.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Quantize whether there's a specific threshold for max_bytes_token where vector-tiling-v1 becomes net-negative across model sizes — propose automated regression sweep across 3–100 byte thresholds.
- Explore whether tokenizer pre-normalization (NFKC reduction of emoji sequences) at the edge yields lower quality regressions than kernel perturbations — short A/B required.
- Instrumentation: add a low-overhead per-request tokenization fingerprint into our sampling pipeline to correlate with SLO breaches in production.
- Long-term: consider unified kernel heuristics that look at token byte-distribution before deciding tiling strategy (cheap approximate estimator).

Action items (owners):
- Maya Chen: schedule automated sweep over byte-thresholds across models S-3, M-7, L-13; add regression job to shadowbench (due 2026-04-21).
- Arjun Patel: prototype edge tokenization fingerprint header and edge pad logic (POC in edge-extras repo) (due 2026-04-19).
- Lena Rodriguez: follow-up microbench comparing lane-pack-v2 across different instance types (A100 vs H100), produce cost/latency trade-off note (due 2026-04-26).
- Noah Fisher: file kernel PR to expose tiling heuristic telemetry counters (PR draft linked).

Notes for docs / exec summary:
- Short executive summary: small prompts with complex unicode (emoji/CJK/multi-byte tokens) interact with low-precision kernels to amplify tail latency via extra tiling/kernel launches. Immediate mitigations (edge pad or kernel config selection) reduce P99 without changing models. Long-term fix is to make kernel tiling heuristics aware of token byte-distribution early in the pipeline.

Attachments: raw traces (linked in linked_artifacts), sample tokenizer histograms, microbench CSVs.

Design considerations for productization:
- If we add a feature to auto-pad at the edge, ensure customer-configured opt-out and quality-safe guards (do not pad prompt tokens that could meaningfully change generated output).
- For Dedicated/Private customers allow toggling kernel preference per-model via the model config API; default to lane-pack-v2 for models with >5% non-latin traffic sampled over 24h.

End of probe note.
